concepts.description: A highly engaging, high-flow activity can keep drawing time and attention well past the point of being net-positive, silently overdrawing other capacity dimensions and commitments because felt absorption in the moment doesn't signal the overdraw the way fatigue on a less engaging task would.
concepts.title: Absorbing Activities Crowd Out Other Commitments

concepts.description: When mood is depressed, wanting to act often follows doing, not the other way around — so pacing plans must schedule small actions as experiments rather than waiting for felt readiness.
concepts.title: Action Before Motivation in Low Mood

concepts.description: Entering a stress-activated state is fast and spreads system-wide, while recovering from it is slower and propagates more selectively, so recovery time is not the mirror image of activation time.
concepts.title: Activation and Recovery Have Asymmetric Rates

concepts.description: Fatigue from inadequate recovery between demands (acute) and from accumulated shortfalls over time (chronic) both reduce performance headroom, but chronic fatigue is easier to underestimate because impairment creeps in gradually and often goes unnoticed.
concepts.title: Acute and Chronic Fatigue

concepts.description: Physical depletion — hunger, fatigue, poor sleep, illness — shrinks effective mental capacity because the brain cannot regulate well from a physically bankrupt body.
concepts.title: Body Budget as Cognitive Baseline

concepts.description: Masking load often begins before a social event (planning, rehearsal) and continues after it (recovery, decompression), so the true capacity cost spans a wider window than the visible interaction alone.
concepts.title: Camouflaging Extends Demand Beyond the Interaction

concepts.description: When demand approaches saturation, only three families of response exist — add capacity, adjust limits by removing stressors, or remove load — and the right mix depends on how close to yield the person already was.
concepts.title: Capacity Load Triage Menu

concepts.description: Demand on a person can increase with manageable compensation up to a yield point, beyond which functioning degrades permanently for that episode until load is removed and recovery completes.
concepts.title: Capacity Yield Point

concepts.description: Sustained absorbed engagement requires task difficulty calibrated just above current skill — too easy leaves spare capacity that wanders, too hard produces overwhelm, and the band shifts upward as skill grows.
concepts.title: Challenge-Skill Balance

concepts.description: Poorly managed teamwork can consume most of the working day in meetings and interruptions, leaving no blocks large enough for deep work and distributing collaborative load unevenly onto a few people.
concepts.title: Collaboration Overload as Hidden Demand

concepts.description: Recovering from acute stress load requires physiologically discharging the accumulated stress-response energy, not merely removing the trigger that caused it.
concepts.title: Completing the Stress-Response Cycle

concepts.description: Holding a fixed wake time and a deliberately bounded sleep window — then expanding bedtime only after sleep quality improves — rebuilds sleep as a reliable capacity-restoration channel faster than varying schedule by how tired you feel each night.
concepts.title: Consistent Sleep Window Protocol

concepts.description: Unaddressed saturation in one dimension of capacity does not stay contained there — it degrades headroom in other dimensions even though the demand on those other dimensions hasn't changed.
concepts.title: Cross-Dimensional Saturation Cascade

concepts.description: Splitting the day into bounded segments gives multiple fresh starts when one block goes poorly, countering the trap of writing off an entire day after a bad morning.
concepts.title: Day Quadrants Instead of All-or-Nothing Days

concepts.description: Cognitively demanding work typically needs several consecutive uninterrupted hours before the effort pays off, so schedules fragmented below that threshold systematically waste capacity on restart cost.
concepts.title: Deep-Work Minimum Block Size

concepts.description: Handing off tasks others can do better or cheaper frees attention for work only you can do — refusing to delegate is often a capacity problem disguised as virtue or control.
concepts.title: Delegation as Capacity Multiplier

concepts.description: Fatigue from low mood is not ordinary tiredness — resting often deepens it — so the capacity move when mood is flat is short, scheduled activity, not more downtime.
concepts.title: Depressed Fatigue Calls for Activity Not Rest

concepts.description: Treating recurring sensory, energy, and social limits as real constraints to design commitments around — rather than as failures to overcome — prevents the repeated overshoot-and-crash pattern that comes from ignoring them.
concepts.title: Designing Around Capacity Limits

concepts.description: Recovery is more effective when the recovery activity targets the same dimension that was actually depleted, rather than defaulting to a generic notion of "rest."
concepts.title: Dimension-Matched Recovery

concepts.description: Personal capacity is better modelled as several independently-saturating dimensions — sensory, physical, emotional, cognitive, and social — than as one undifferentiated pool of energy.
concepts.title: Dimensions of Personal Capacity

concepts.description: When social cues are not absorbed automatically through mirror-neuron simulation, the brain must actively decode tone, expression, and implied meaning — adding a continuous cognitive tax on top of the interaction itself.
concepts.title: Effortful Social Mentalizing Tax

concepts.description: Some brains run a higher resting cognitive "noise" level and maintain more neural connections than typical, so capacity is spent on baseline upkeep before any task demand is added — the same energy pool that fuels deliberate thinking also funds that idle overhead.
concepts.title: Elevated Baseline Cognitive Idle Cost

concepts.description: Colour-coding tasks by energy cost and matching them to the day's available energy — not just available time — prevents planning that assumes full headroom every morning.
concepts.title: Energy-Rated Task Lists

concepts.description: A struggle that looks like a fixed personal deficit can instead be a demand/capacity mismatch created by the environment; changing the environment to match actual capacity can resolve the struggle entirely without any change in underlying skill.
concepts.title: Environmental Mismatch as the Source of Disabling Struggle

concepts.description: Previewing a new place or route before full exposure converts abstract unpredictability into processed detail, lowering the spike load of first-time environments.
concepts.title: Environmental Trial Run Before Novel Demands

concepts.description: Under sustained load, people often shed optional nourishing activities first while keeping obligatory stressors — narrowing life until only depleting demands remain and capacity spirals down further.
concepts.title: Exhaustion Funnel From Dropping Nourishing Activities

concepts.description: Deliberately keeping a stock of low-variance, already-evaluated choices (a routine, a "safe" option) for use when headroom is low avoids spending scarce capacity on evaluating novelty, at the cost of variety.
concepts.title: Fallback to Known-Cost Options Under Load

concepts.description: Effortful mental work including self-control measurably draws down blood glucose, and restoring it can prevent the performance drop that otherwise follows a depleting task.
concepts.title: Glucose and Effortful Cognition

concepts.description: When available capacity is low, success depends on decomposing demands into steps small enough to complete at the current level — including time-boxed goals — rather than matching neurotypical task size.
concepts.title: Graded Task Decomposition for Low Headroom

concepts.description: A demand's capacity cost is not fixed by its surface-level content alone — a stressor that lands on an unresolved past wound draws substantially more capacity than the same stressor would otherwise, because present distress compounds with old, unprocessed distress.
concepts.title: Historical Sensitization Amplifies Demand Cost

concepts.description: Deep absorption can suppress hunger, bathroom, and clock cues until crisis level — adding a hidden recovery cost and requiring external timers when internal signals are unreliable.
concepts.title: Hyperfocus Bypasses Interoception and Time

concepts.description: A coping skill developed in one context can be repurposed for capacity pacing elsewhere by stripping it to its active ingredient and reapplying that mechanism across dimensions or disabilities.
concepts.title: Identify-Isolate-Transfer for Pacing

concepts.description: Given several ways to reach the same goal, people gravitate toward the least attention-demanding path — effort is a cost in the economy of action, and this bias shapes both habit formation and capacity planning.
concepts.title: Law of Least Effort

concepts.description: Attention is a finite resource allocated across activities, and effortful tasks interfere with each other when their combined demand exceeds that budget — even when each task alone seems manageable.
concepts.title: Limited Attention Budget

concepts.description: A three-part pacing cycle — fund baseline capacity, shed guilt and excess demand, then restore motivation through interest-matched input — coordinates prevention, demand reduction, and replenishment instead of treating any one as sufficient alone.
concepts.title: Maintain-Recover-Reload Cycle

concepts.description: Suppressing natural self-regulating behaviour to appear "fine" consumes capacity on top of the task itself, so the visible task load understates true demand.
concepts.title: Masking as a Hidden Capacity Drain

concepts.description: Holding the body still through sustained muscular effort — not relaxed calm — consumes capacity continuously, so "sitting quietly" can be more demanding than visible movement.
concepts.title: Movement Suppression as Hidden Capacity Drain

concepts.description: A model in which a person's nervous system absorbs sensory, social, and informational input with less internal filtering, so their capacity depletes faster than a "typical" baseline would predict.
concepts.title: Nervous-System-on-the-Outside Load Model

concepts.description: The same category of activity can be net-depleting or net-restorative depending on whether it fits the person's sensory, social, and physical preferences, not on the activity category itself.
concepts.title: Net Capacity Effect Depends on Activity Fit

concepts.description: Daily activities differ in net capacity effect — some refill headroom, others drain it — and pacing requires auditing the mix, not only total hours busy or free.
concepts.title: Nourishing Versus Depleting Activity Balance

concepts.description: Focused output is maximized within a personal range of ambient stimulation rather than simply below a ceiling — both under- and over-stimulation degrade functioning, so headroom management has to guard a floor as well as a cap.
concepts.title: Optimal Stimulation Range

concepts.description: When total demand exceeds sustainable load, output often alternates between hyperfocused overdelivery and bare-minimum shutdown — looking like inconsistency but reflecting a capacity problem, not capability.
concepts.title: Oscillating Performance Under Overload

concepts.description: Deciding in advance, while headroom is available, which demands can be dropped and under what circumstances avoids having to spend scarce evaluation capacity on that decision during a period of low headroom.
concepts.title: Precommitted Demand-Shedding

concepts.description: Scheduling recovery periods before saturation is reached is more effective than taking recovery only reactively after a breakdown, because by the time reactive recovery is triggered the deficit is already much larger.
concepts.title: Proactive Recovery Scheduling

concepts.description: Not all activities that look or feel like rest actually restore capacity; some give fleeting relief while leaving net capacity lower, so recovery value must be measured by actual rejuvenation, not by social convention or immediate gratification.
concepts.title: Restorative Rest versus Cheap Rest

concepts.description: Standardizing low-stakes choices (meals, commute, morning sequence) frees executive and decision capacity for demands that actually vary, especially when the baseline depletion rate is already high.
concepts.title: Routine as Decision-Capacity Preservation

concepts.description: Repetitive dwelling on guilt, sadness, or self-directed anger consumes capacity continuously in the background — not only during focused tasks — so headroom can shrink even when nothing new is being done.
concepts.title: Rumination as Continuous Cognitive Demand

concepts.description: Capacity availability varies predictably across the day for a given person, so scheduling demanding work against that individual pattern uses fewer total hours to produce more usable output than scheduling by uniform clock time.
concepts.title: Schedule Around Energy Patterns, Not Just Clock Time

concepts.description: Confining a recurring, capacity-consuming activity to one fixed time window and deferring intrusions outside it prevents that demand from draining capacity continuously throughout the day.
concepts.title: Scheduled Batching of Recurring Demand

concepts.description: When work and personal time share the same space, explicitly scheduling stressful obligations and separating work channels from personal ones frees off-hours rest from the feeling that relaxation is slacking.
concepts.title: Scheduled Work Boundaries for Guilt-Free Rest

concepts.description: Planning each demand as a standalone block without modeling how deficits accumulate across a sequence systematically under-counts end-of-period fatigue and recovery need.
concepts.title: Scheduling Isolated Blocks Underestimates Cumulative Load

concepts.description: Baseline routines that fund physical and cognitive capacity are preventive maintenance — done before the day starts so breakdown is less likely — not luxury "self-care" reserved for after everything else is finished.
concepts.title: Self-Maintenance as Preventive Capacity Work

concepts.description: After voluntary-effort depletion, specific inputs — rest breaks, glucose, exercise, rewards, and positive affect — restore the shared self-regulation budget faster than simply waiting.
concepts.title: Factors That Replenish the Self-Regulatory Pool

concepts.description: Self-control, deliberate thought, and other voluntary effort draw on a common limited budget, so spending it on one demand leaves less for the next even when the tasks look unrelated.
concepts.title: Shared Pool of Voluntary Effort

concepts.description: As skill in a task grows, the same performance requires less attention and less physiological effort — a key mechanism by which practice increases effective headroom without raising raw capacity limits.
concepts.title: Skill Reduces Cognitive Demand

concepts.description: Sleep is a primary channel for overnight capacity restoration, so a sleep shortfall doesn't just cause tiredness — it directly degrades next-day cognitive and emotional headroom, compounding the deficit.
concepts.title: Sleep Debt Compounds Across Dimensions

concepts.description: Social interaction draws on a limited, individually-sized pool of social capacity that depletes faster under high-pressure formats and recovers only with time alone or lower-cost connection.
concepts.title: Social Energy as Spendable Capacity

concepts.description: Self-stimulatory movement, sound, or touch can offload sensory and emotional load in the moment — restoring attention and preventing escalation — so suppressing stims raises true demand on top of the task.
concepts.title: Stimming as Real-Time Capacity Regulation

concepts.description: Deliberately operating below maximum perceived effort, rather than at it, sustains higher output over time than an intermittent maximum-effort/crash cycle, because running without margin leaves no headroom to absorb variance or recover.
concepts.title: Sustainable Effort Margin

concepts.description: Moving between dissimilar tasks incurs a refocusing cost on top of the tasks' own demand, and this switching cost is amplified for some people, making batching similar work a distinct capacity-saving lever from reducing task count.
concepts.title: Task-Switching Cost

concepts.description: Keeping one sensory or attention constant across a task change softens the cost of moving from rest to action or from one activity to another when inertia makes both starts and stops expensive.
concepts.title: Transition Bridges for Autistic Inertia

concepts.description: Baseline vagal tone governs how flexibly the nervous system adapts to and recovers from stress, and functions as a trainable parameter of the recovery rate itself rather than a fixed trait.
concepts.title: Vagal Tone as a Determinant of Recovery Capacity

concepts.description: Imprecise requests force extra computation to infer what, when, and why before work can start — a hidden attention cost that literal thinkers and anyone under load pay disproportionately.
concepts.title: Vague Instructions Amplify Cognitive Demand

concepts.description: A later appointment can consume the whole day in anxious limbo when working memory, hyperfocus risk, time blindness, and decision paralysis combine — leaving no productive headroom before the event even starts.
concepts.title: Waiting Mode Locks Capacity Before Events

concepts.description: A model of saturation as a bounded operating zone with two failure thresholds — hyperarousal above it, hypoarousal below it — whose width is itself a capacity parameter that varies by person and can be trained.
concepts.title: Window of Tolerance

concepts.description: Working memory holds and manipulates information for immediate use, and its effective capacity shrinks when other demands — masking, sensory processing, anxiety — already occupy slots in the same buffer.
concepts.title: Working Memory as Cognitive Capacity Buffer

concepts.description: Adjusting schedule, workload intensity, and continuity of employment — not just where work happens — lets people align demand with their actual capacity curve instead of forcing a single pattern on everyone.
concepts.title: Workload Flexibility as a Capacity Lever
